questions.explanation: Renaissance fronts stack orders by height, plainest below and richest above. The piano nobile takes the middle order, so its scroll capitals read as Ionic rather than Tuscan or Corinthian.

questions.topic: The symmetry of a Palladian plan
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a symmetrical plan reads as balanced on uneven ground
questions.stem: Explain why a villa with a sloping site still reads to the eye as a balanced composition.

answer.exemplar: A Palladian villa is arranged on a single central axis with matching rooms and equal wings set at the same distance on either side, so the drawing is a mirror of itself. The eye reads that geometric arrangement, and a gentle fall in the ground does not disturb the symmetry of the plan.

questions.explanation: Symmetry on paper lets the eye read the villa as two mirrored halves, so uneven ground does not disturb it. The bays and the plan's wings are laid out around one central axis.
questions.hint: Think of the plan as a diagram, not a photograph.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the structural frame that replaced load-bearing walls

stimulus.body: A note pinned to the planner's board describes a hall where the roof rests on a lattice of slender clustered piers and beams rather than on the walls. The note asks which earlier arrangement the lattice took over from.

questions.stem: According to the board note, what did the lattice of piers and beams take over from?

options.text: Load-bearing walls, whose own thickness had to carry the roof and resist its push
Vaults spanning bay by bay, which the lattice left standing and in use
options.misconception: believes vaults stayed the chief spanning device

options.text: Buttressing piers outside the building, which the lattice removed from the exterior
options.misconception: thinks flying buttresses were the frame's predecessor

options.text: Arcades of solid piers, which the lattice permanently covered and replaced
options.misconception: assumes the arcades were entirely superseded

questions.explanation: The frame carries the roof load down to the foundations, so the walls become thin curtains rather than the support. It therefore takes over from thick load-bearing walls, not from vaults, buttresses or arcades.
questions.hint: Ask what the walls themselves now have to do.

The main support, holding up the roof once the frame is in place
options.misconception: believes the skin still carries the roof

options.misconception: confuses a curtain wall with a buttress

options.text: A sealed edge, closed on every side with no openings at all
options.misconception: thinks a curtain wall must be blank

questions.explanation: Two-stage reasoning: the first step fixes the wall as a skin, and the second asks what follows once a separate frame takes the loads. The wall then only shelters and encloses the space behind it.

options.misconception: assumes heavy walls are later infill

The 0.4 metre Renaissance wall, since a thin modern build is always stronger

questions.topic: Reading a wall as structure
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a load-bearing wall from a curtain wall in a single view
questions.stem: Explain how you could tell a load-bearing wall from a curtain wall using one photograph of a building.

answer.exemplar: Look at the openings first. A load-bearing wall is deep and has small, scattered openings such as slits or paired windows, because the wall is resisting the push of the vaults inside. A curtain wall is thin, regular and can carry a long glazed band or a row of equal windows, since a frame behind it carries the loads and the wall only encloses.

questions.explanation: The clearest clues are depth and the size and rhythm of the openings. Small scattered openings in a deep wall signal structural duty, while long glazed bands in a thin wall signal a frame behind.
questions.hint: Start with the size of the openings.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a curtain wall frees the plan from structural constraints
questions.stem: Explain how the presence of a curtain wall changes what an architect can decide about a floor plan.

answer.exemplar: Because a curtain wall carries no load, the frame can be set on a regular grid while the enclosure is placed wherever the rooms need it, including a glazed wall in the middle of the plan where a medieval builder would have had to build a solid mass. The plan is therefore settled by how the building is used, and not by where the supports happen to land.

questions.explanation: With the load carried by a frame, the enclosure has no structural duty, so the plan is set by use rather than by where supports must land. Openings can move, widen and fill with glass.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The frame that made height possible
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a frame allows a building to exceed load-bearing wall heights
questions.stem: Explain how the arrival of a structural frame let buildings rise higher than load-bearing walls allowed.

answer.exemplar: A load-bearing wall must be thick enough to resist the outward push of the roof and vaults above it, and it grows heavier and less stable as it rises, so there is a height beyond which such walls cannot stand. A frame takes those loads down through slender columns to the foundations, which means the height of the building is limited by the strength of the columns and their bracing rather than by the bulk of the walls.

questions.explanation: Height with bearing walls is limited by the need for ever thicker, heavier walls, while a frame carries the same loads down slender members. The limit on height therefore moves from wall bulk to frame strength.
questions.hint: Compare what gets thicker as the building rises.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how Baroque planning controls the sequence of views
questions.stem: Explain how Baroque planning turns a building into a series of controlled views rather than a single display.

answer.exemplar: Instead of opening the whole building at once, a Baroque plan sequences the visit. The entrance gives a compressed or partly hidden view, a corridor turns the visitor so that the next room appears from an angle, and each room offers a different picture through its own window, arch or oval opening. The visitor is therefore given one image at a time, and the drama depends on the order in which those images arrive.

questions.explanation: Baroque plans sequence the visit, giving one framed image at a time instead of a single overall view. Compression, turning corridors and shaped openings all control what is seen and when.
questions.hint: Think about what the visitor is not allowed to see yet.

questions.stem: Explain how a cruciform plan lets a church hold a large congregation while keeping its sanctuary clear.

answer.exemplar: The arms of the cross give the building a long nave for the congregation and a wide transept for overflow, while the eastern arm stays a distinct and separate space for the clergy and the altar. Because the congregation gathers in the nave and the transept rather than in front of the sanctuary, the sanctuary can keep a clear axis and a calm focus of its own.

questions.explanation: The long nave and the wide transept hold the congregation, while the eastern arm remains a separate sanctuary with a clear axis. The cross shape therefore divides crowd from altar without separating the building.
questions.hint: Ask where the people go and where the altar stays.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The orders applied to a Renaissance palace
questions.learningObjective: Compute an entablature height from the column it sits on
questions.stem: A planner's diagram gives a column 4 metres tall and states that its entablature is one and a fifth times the height of the column. How tall is the entablature in metres?
questions.explanation: One and a fifth of 4 metres is 4.8 metres, so the entablature sits above the shaft at that height. The rule works because the entablature is measured from the same column the ratio was set against.
questions.hint: Multiply the column height by one and a fifth.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: The symmetry of a Palladian plan
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a mirrored room supports a villa's balanced plan

stimulus.body: A note on the planner's board describes a room whose plan, openings and even the position of its fireplace are the exact mirror of the room opposite it across the central hall. The note asks how the room is read by a visitor.

questions.stem: According to the note, how does the described room read to a visitor of the villa?

options.text: As one half of a matched pair, which makes the room a visible part of the whole plan
As a service room, since matched pairs are kept apart from the main house
options.misconception: reads the mirror as a service arrangement

options.text: As a later addition, because an exact mirror is never part of a first design
options.misconception: treats the mirror as evidence of a later date

options.text: As a free alteration, since the room ignores the axis of the villa
options.misconception: claims the room ignores the axis

questions.explanation: A room that mirrors its opposite is visibly a half of a pair, so the symmetry of the plan is legible from inside the building as well as on the drawing. Such a room confirms the axis rather than ignoring it.
questions.hint: Look at what the room matches across the hall.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: A Baroque plan and the route through it
questions.learningObjective: Connect a curved room's geometry to the movement it produces
questions.stem: First: name the kind of room whose plan is a smooth curve rather than a rectangle. Second: what does that geometry do to the movement of visitors?

options.text: An oval hall, which drives circulation around the centre instead of across the room
A barrel-vaulted hall, which drives visitors straight along its central axis
options.misconception: confuses a curved plan with a vaulted space

options.text: A gallery, which drives visitors forward along a straight painted sequence
options.misconception: links the curved plan to a straight gallery

options.text: A narthex, which drives visitors into the body of the church and no further
options.misconception: uses the porch for a curving hall

questions.explanation: The first step names the oval hall, and the second asks what its geometry does: doors set around the curve turn circulation into a loop around the middle of the room rather than a straight crossing.
questions.hint: The shape of the plan is the first answer.
